records.title: Topological sort of dependency graph
Support schemas with recursive references
records.body:
There are several issues with this.

1. The parser needs to be able to handle infinite schemas. This likely means instantiating default elements and keeping track of them, and then recursing through and setting attributes. There is a POC of this in `feature/recursive-schema`.
2. The orderer needs to be able to identify cycles, and either annotate them for manual resolution in the output or resolve them as is.
3. The DSL itself needs to be able to handle infinite recursion. This chiefly causes problems in places with default values. If the default value is the element with no arguments, but some properties have defaults, then instantiating with no arguments will trigger an infinite recursion.

What is the correct way to write recursive schemas in the DSL?
```python
class TreeNode(Object):
    parent = Property(Element())

TreeNode.properties["value"].element = TreeNode
```
or maybe
```python
class TreeNode(Object):
    parent = Property(lambda: TreeNode)
```

records.title: Add support for Recursive CTEs 🚀
records.body:
### Description

Would love support for recursive CTEs via the `rust sql api`. My use case requires calculations/columns that recursively depend on themselves over some dimension (think compounding growth or beg and ending bank balances over time). As of now, I have to resort to using `duckdb-rs`. 

Example 

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE GrowthCTE AS (
      -- Base case
      SELECT 1 as Index, CAST(100 as FLOAT4) AS Value
      UNION ALL
      -- Recursive step
      SELECT
          Index + 1,
          Value * 1.08
      FROM GrowthCTE
      WHERE Index < 10 
  )
  SELECT
      Index,
      Value
  FROM GrowthCTE;
```

results in the error 

```bash
Error: ComputeError(ErrString("Recursive CTEs are not supported"))
```

records.title: Proposal: Common Table Expressions and Recursive Queries
records.body:
Sequelize currently has no support for common table expressions and recursive CTEs. Adding the ability to include a CTE into the find* family of methods would allow find* to perform recursive queries. To see some examples of situations where this would be helpful skip to the "Examples" section at the end of the proposal.
# CTE Background

Before we get into the API proposal the following is some information about CTEs and how they work.
## Common Table Expressions

A common table expression is a temporary result that lasts only as long as the query it accompanies, can reference itself, and can be referenced multiple times from the query it is part of. The general form of a CTE is a table name definition, column name definitions, and a SELECT statement.
## Recursive CTEs

A recursive cte follows the same guidelines as a normal CTE, but has an additional SELECT statement. In a recursive CTE the first SELECT is called the initial select and the second is called the recursive select.
The following procedure is followed when running a recursive CTE.
1. The initial selection is made and added to a queue
2. While the queue is not empty
   1. Pull a single row from the queue
   2. Add it to the recursive selection table
   3. Perform the recursive select, but only on the single added row
   4. Add the results of the recursive selection to the queue

When a query uses a recursive CTE it becomes a recursive query.
# API Proposal

To allow CTEs through the Sequelize API add a new optional `cte` property to the `options` argument of the find* family of methods. `cte` will describe one or more CTEs that will be part of the find. To support some common use cases of recursive queries new methods will also need to be added to `Sequelize` to represent binary SQL operators.
## `cte` option

The new optional property `cte` is a array of plain objects that each represent a CTE, from now on referred to as `cte objects`.
### Ordinary `cte objects`

Each `cte object` is required to have a single property, `name`. `name` is simply a title the CTE will use. You may notice that there is no required property that deals with the name and number of columns for the CTE. This is because by default a CTE is selecting `Models` of the type that called the find* method. It will select all attributes of that model, or only the ones given in `attributes`. If a CTE needs to be used for a different model than the model type that called it the property `model` can be given to change the model type of the CTE. It may also be useful to have additional attributes in the CTE. By defining the property `cteAttributes` on a `cte object` as an array of strings the CTE will have an extra attribute for each string, from now on referred to as "additional attributes". It is also possible to specify the `model` as `null`. In this case the CTE will not represent any model and instead will be a custom set of attributes. If `model` is `null` then at least one additional attribute must be defined. 

The `initial` property will describe the selection that fills the CTE. `initial` isn't required if the CTE has a model and no additional attributes because the CTE can select every result and go from there. However, if any additional attributes for the CTE have been defined the `initial` property must be given. For each additional attribute the `initial` property must have a property itself that has the same name. The value of the property will be the selection of the initial attribute. `initial` can also have the `where` and `include` properties to limit the selection of a table.
### Recursive `cte objects`

So far we have only described a ordinary CTE. To use a `cte object` in a recursive way the `recursive` property must be given. As with `initial`, if there are any additional attributes they must be defined through a property in `recursive`. `recursive` has a property, `find`,  that can be used when the CTE is being used with a model. `find` needs to be a string that represents an association (through the `through` property). If `find` is given then the recursive select will automatically create a select that finds the associated instance of the model. The association must be from the model to itself, otherwise the selection will not work. recursive can also use `where`, `include`, `limit`, `offset`, and `order`, with some twists. `where` can use additional attributes, as can `order`. `include` can be used to limit the selection based on a attributes of a associated model, but will not eagerly load the associated model. 

`cte` has another property related to recursion, `unique`. By default when building a recursive CTE, the CTE will not be allowed to have duplicate rows. In the case of CTEs a duplicate row must have identical model attributes and identical additional attributes. However, `unique` can be set to `false` to allow the CTE to contain duplicates. 

There is no guarantee that a recursive CTE will stop selecting. When creating a recursive `cte object` it is important to consider if it has a `find`, `where`, or `include` property that will stop the selection. 
### Using `cte objects` Elsewhere

After a `cte object` is defined it can be used in any subsequent cte or in the find* selection. To access a attribute, simply use the usual Sequelize method, `Sequelize.col("a.attribute")` where a is the name of the CTE and attribute is the name of the attribute. CTEs can only be used in the find method they are defined in.
### Defining CTE attribute values

In some recursive queries it is useful to perform arithmetic in the recursive select, such as incrementing a counter. To assist in these cases objects used to define CTE attributes can have a special objects that references columns and binary operators properties. To reference a column use `{ $col: 'cteName.attribute' }`. This object can be used in combination with numbers and operators to create a select statement. The supported operators are:

| Operator | Type | Description |
| --- | ---

records.title: Failure for table function parameter in recursive query
records.body:
A query involving a recursive CTE containing a table function that takes the recursive reference as a parameter fails with _Column cannot be resolved_

Query:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE t(n, m) AS (
    VALUES(1, 0)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n+1, max(sequential_number) FROM TABLE(sequence(stop => n+1)) WHERE n < 5
)
SELECT * FROM t;
```

Result:

> Query 20231005_152216_00015_daic9 failed: line 4:68: Column 'n' cannot be resolved

Expected Result:

```sql
VALUES(1, 0)
UNION ALL
SELECT 2, max(sequential_number) FROM TABLE(sequence(stop => 2))
UNION ALL
SELECT 3, max(sequential_number) FROM TABLE(sequence(stop => 3))
UNION ALL
SELECT 4, max(sequential_number) FROM TABLE(sequence(stop => 4))

-- Result

 _col0 | _col1 
-------+-------
     1 |     0 
     4 |     4 
     3 |     3 
     2 |     2 
(4 rows)
```
